lines.text: Now the plan. Every twenty milliseconds, the code gets two velocities: the one we have, and the one we want.
It doesn't limit the velocity. It limits the change: how far the velocity may move in this one loop.
Because changing velocity is what takes a push. Cruising at a steady speed costs almost no grip.
At ten meters per second squared, that's two tenths of a meter per second per loop. Small steps, fifty times a second.
Each change goes through three checks, always in this order.
One, the turning cap: the spin may only change so fast.
Two, the motors: when speeding up, ask no more than they can still add at this speed.
Three, traction: driving and turning together must fit inside the grip. If not, shrink both.
Traction goes last, like a referee, because it's the only check that sees driving and turning together.
Whatever survives becomes this loop's command.
In our simulator, these checks left fifteen to thirty percent less odometry error than one fixed limit.
Now let's put real numbers on every check.
